## 2026-11-21 01:52 +0545 — source NACK-cache retention metrics added

- **Existing failure/seam:** the 3,000-pair M7-H run reached 15.06 GB
  HeapAlloc with no final p99. The current source path explains how packet
  allocations can remain live: `TrackRemote.ReadRTP` returns an owned RTP
  packet; `forwardTrack` passes it to `rememberPacket`, which retains it in
  the 512-entry per-track `packetCache`. `handleNACK` reads from that cache.
- **Retention boundary:** subscriber queue entries clone the RTP header while
  sharing the payload; the existing outbound Pion NACK responder is also
  configured for 512 packets. These are distinct retention paths. The source
  inspection identifies a plausible contributor to the `ReadRTP` profile site,
  but does not apportion the M7-H heap or prove the aggregate root cause.
- **Capability increment:** the existing loopback Prometheus endpoint now
  reports active source-cache packet count and RTP payload bytes. Atomic
  accounting follows insertion, same-sequence replacement, and ring eviction.
  The byte gauge excludes packet/header and map overhead, subscriber queues,
  and Pion's responder, so it is not total retained heap and does not change
  packet handling or the protected 512-packet histories.
- **Cheaply killed hypothesis:** lowering Pion's receive MTU changes the
  incoming read-buffer size, not the retained NACK-cache entries, and risks
  truncating larger packets. Changing the OS socket read buffer would not

## 2026-11-20 21:16 +0545 — Safe Pion NACK payload-sharing patch designed

- **Fresh upstream check:** `github.com/pion/interceptor v0.1.51` remains the
  latest release checked. Current upstream `main` at
  `0353a584d11ccb4ca5f9e4e59d78c87b0830ed11` still exposes `DisableCopy` and
  stream filtering, but no packet-factory injection. In v0.1.51,
  `ResponderInterceptor.packetFactory` is private and defaults to
  `NewPacketFactoryCopy`.
- **Ownership proof:** Pion WebRTC v4.2.26's `TrackLocalStaticRTP.WriteRTP`
  copies the packet into a pooled `rtp.Packet` and resets that object after
  writing. `PacketFactoryNoOp` retains the address of that pooled header, so
  it can observe a later packet's header; this is why plain `DisableCopy()`
  is not acceptable. The Hami payload path is different: its source packet
  comes from `TrackRemote.ReadRTP`, is retained by the existing track cache,
  and is not mutated while queued or retransmitted.
- **Existing integration seam:** WebRTC v4.2.26 already exposes
  `RegisterDefaultInterceptorsWithOptions` and `WithNackResponderOptions`;
  a future Pion responder option can therefore be selected without replacing
  the rest of the default interceptor chain. The existing router API
  construction sites in `services/hami-media/main.go` are the Hami call seam.
- **Candidate design (not implemented):** add an opt-in responder packet
  factory that clones each RTP header but shares the immutable payload for
  non-RTX packets. If either RTX SSRC or RTX payload type is present, delegate
  to the existing `PacketFactoryCopy` so SSRC/PT/sequence rewriting, original
  sequence prefixing, and padding handling remain unchanged. Reuse Pion's
  existing `RetainablePacket` reference count and `RTPBuffer` eviction/release;
  do not add a separate refcount/cache. Select the option only for router APIs
  behind a default-off build flag; publisher/viewer APIs and the default
  responder remain unchanged.
- **Acceptance tests:** Pion factory tests must verify independent cloned
  headers, shared payload backing storage, safe release/eviction, and exact
  RTX fallback rewriting. Then run the existing
  `TestLocalSFURoutesAuthorizedStreamsAndRTCP` with the flag enabled and
  require NACK/PLI/FIR plus a viewer retransmission. Only after that, rebuild
  a fresh counters-on 20x50 control before treatment; require no worse
  p95/p99, frame completeness, queue drops, write errors, or RTCP behavior.
- **New-file rationale before any fork:** inspected Hami's router API creation
  in `main.go` and Pion's existing `responder_option.go`,
  `responder_interceptor.go`, and `internal/rtpbuffer/packet_factory.go`.
  Hami cannot set the responder's private factory or import Pion's `internal`
  factory implementation. A reproducible candidate therefore needs a
  versioned local Pion module replacement; its new source files would carry
  that patched dependency, while modifications to Hami's existing files alone
  cannot implement the required option. The current order still forbids
  commit/push, so no fork files or non-buildable Hami call sites were created.
- **Current result:** design only; no source patch, Go build, focused SFU test,
  or load run in this phase. `npm test` passed (168 script and 295 TypeScript
  tests); `npm run gates` was GREEN. The pre-existing generated timestamp
  change in `docs/GATES.md` was preserved. Prior Hami ring candidate remains
  not adopted; its 20x50 verdicts are in the preceding entry. No protected
  setting changed.
- **Next:** when a versioned local dependency patch can be carried under the
  repository's new-file/commit-description rule, implement this default-off
  option in the existing Pion seams, prove RTX fallback and the focused

  like a way to remove the 3.82 GB per-viewer `PacketFactoryCopy` cost, but
  pinned WebRTC v4.2.26's `TrackLocalStaticRTP.WriteRTP` obtains a pooled

  optimization and was not adopted. The public responder option does not

## 2026-11-19 22:43 +0545 — CONFIRMED: why the gate-checks loop fails — d34's own line is the diff

- **Mechanism CONFIRMED (file lists browser-verified 22:42):** d34a6acdb changed 3 files — docs/GATES.md, docs/WHO_DID_WHAT.md, AND scripts/who-did-what.mjs. Because d34 touched the generator script (a non-report file), d34 is NOT report-only under the generator's rule (a commit is dropped only if ALL its files are in {CAPABILITY_QUEUE.md, GATES.md, WHO_DID_WHAT.md}). aeae2a4 changed only docs/CAPABILITY_QUEUE.md — it IS report-only and was correctly excluded.
- **Why CI fails:** the committed report (generated at d34 time, before d34 was in the log) EXCLUDES d34 — verified by grep: d34a6ac occurs 0 times in docs/WHO_DID_WHAT.md, as do aeae2a4/436bd0e/2dcd3c5/cdcebdc; newest listed agent commit is d55d4e4. CI regenerates with `npm run who-did-what -- --exclude-head` (git log HEAD^) at aeae2a4, which INCLUDES d34. Regenerated file != committed file → `WHO_DID_WHAT.md is stale` → gate-checks fails. The 22:39 entry's "exclusion incomplete" framing is corrected: the exclusion works; the stale diff is d34's own missing line.
- **Fix (reasoned from the script + workflow, to be proven by a CI run):** run PLAIN `npm run who-did-what` (NO --exclude-head) at HEAD=aeae2a4 so the report includes d34, and commit ONLY docs/WHO_DID_WHAT.md as a report-only commit. CI at that commit regenerates with --exclude-head → same set (d34 in, head out) → should PASS. Prove locally with the exact CI command before pushing. This one plain regeneration is NOT another loop refresh — the loop-causing pattern was refreshes generated with --exclude-head (or at the parent HEAD), which exclude the very code commit they must include.
- **Durability warning:** this holds only until the commit after the next code commit — after every code commit, a plain refresh must land before the following commit's CI, or the check must stop gating on the report (fix-order option 2). The fix worker must state which durability path it takes.

## 2026-11-19 21:27 +0545 — remove per-packet subscriber-slice allocation

- **Existing seam and why:** `sfuRouter.forwardTrack` in
  `services/hami-media/main.go` previously copied every track subscriber
  map into a new slice for each received RTP packet. This was the only
  per-packet subscriber-slice allocation in that loop. `subscribe`,
  `unsubscribe`, and track-unregistration remain the existing mutation seam.
- **Change:** `forwardTrack` now holds the existing `r.mu.RLock` and iterates
  `source.subscribers` directly. It enqueues under each subscription's existing
  lock, aggregates the first write error and one recovery subscription, then
  releases `r.mu` before requesting the keyframe or recording router errors.
  This preserves the old lock direction and avoids an inverse `r.mu`/error
  lock while enqueueing.
- **Evidence:** local Go validation passed:
  `cd services/hami-media && go test ./...`,
  `go vet ./...`, `go build -o /tmp/hami-media-subscriber-map-opt .`, and
  `go test -race ./...`. The build is local-only at
  `/tmp/hami-media-subscriber-map-opt`.
- **Measured delta:** per-RTP subscriber-slice allocation removed in source.
  A repeatable CPU/heap/viewer-minute A/B is not yet measured; do not claim
  a throughput or cost improvement from this source change alone.
- **Next kill rule:** run the existing local 250/500/1,000 M7-H harness with
  this binary and a clean no-change control, preserving NACK, queue-drop,
  write-error, recovery, and cleanup contracts. Docker Desktop is currently

## 2026-11-19 19:03 +0545 — local multi-instance sharding screen did not lower CPU cost

- **Existing seam and scope:** ran the existing M7-H binary as one local
  1,000-viewer harness/SFU pair, then as two independent 500-viewer pairs and
  four independent 250-viewer pairs. This is a process-partition screening
  measurement, not a single M7-H proof routed across multiple SFUs; no source
  or deployment code changed. Each run used the same no-dissolve baseline
  binary, normal inter-frame fixture, 60-second duration, and local-only mode.
- **Per-process samples:** CPU is the first-to-nearest-60s
  `processCPUSeconds` delta, normalized by the sampled wall interval and total
  viewer-minutes; HeapAlloc and goroutines are the corresponding end-window

## 2026-11-19 — M7-H mux-off profile comparison (011 follow-on)

- **Existing seam:** ran `go tool pprof -top -nodecount=20` and
  `go tool pprof -traces -lines` on all four mux-off profiles and the four
  mux-on baseline profiles; grouped traces by their pprof separators. Full
  counts and stacks are in `/tmp/hami-media-011-muxoff-pprof.md`.
- **Measured path shift:** mux-on SFU's largest fd-write-lock/NACK group was
  23,051 at stall and 25,589 at follow-up through
  `UDPMuxDefault.writeToContext`. All mux-off profiles have zero
  `UDPMuxDefault` stacks. At mux-off stall, the largest harness group is
  32,544 on `fdMutex.rwlock` -> per-connection `UDPConn.WriteToUDPAddrPort`
  -> ICE `CandidatePair.Write` -> NACK resend; its aggregate NACK-resend
  stack count is 37,602. The SFU has 6,836 fd-write-lock stacks, including
  1,844 during STUN keepalive, while its largest group is 12,000 packet-buffer
  reads. At the follow-up, fd-write-lock counts fall to 1 (harness) and 0
  (SFU); 12,000 packet-buffer reads are the largest group in both.
- **Interpretation / uncertainty:** mux removal changes the visible writer
  path but does not prevent the full stall. The evidence supports transient
  per-connection UDP write contention under ICE/NACK load, but cannot
  attribute it uniquely to Pion writer behavior versus host loopback/kernel
  backpressure. Follow-up captures are 31/32 seconds after initial mux-off
  profiles versus 43/54 seconds for mux-on; avoid direct temporal conclusions.
- **Single next test:** same 3,000/3,000 mux-off diagnostic run, but bypass
  only Pion's NACK `ResponderInterceptor` on harness publisher peers; preserve
  every other setting and capture the same counters/profiles. Disappearance
  of both the NACK/fdMutex cohort and zero-frame/all-stale signature supports
  NACK-driven write pressure; persistence kills NACK retransmission as a
  necessary trigger and points next to ICE receive/host loopback behavior.
  This proposed test was not run and is not acceptance evidence.
- **Owner dependency / boundary:** no routine owner action or economic
  dependency was removed; `OWNER_INTERVENTIONS_PER_REAL_TRANSACTION` remains
  **NOT MEASURABLE**. No code or protected constant changed, and no commit,

  at every level, and loses worse as the penalty rises (-8, -29, -58). Do NOT sweep it
  further. Loop reduction alone does NOT win. (Loop counts independently verified by
  the 00:13 self-watch run from the gen files: strict loop rows base 8/50 -> pen 1.1
  3/50 -> pen 1.2 0/50; not re-counted in this run. The verdict does not depend on
  the counts.)
- **Layer probe v3 ANSWERED (19:00 UTC, /tmp/layer-probe3.log; full table + caveat in
  /tmp/weight-space-experiment-4-base-loops.md §3):** the offset-mapping fix worked —
  13 spans of the 14-token loop phrase found on row 535. The loop lock is a LATE-layer
  phenomenon (layers ~22-35): loop-phrase hidden-state similarity dips to 0.918
  mid-network (layer 21) then recovers to 0.997 at the final layer (35), while the
  control word falls to 0.826-0.84. Largest loop-vs-control gap at layer 35 (+0.155).
  The collapse spans ~10 late layers, not one layer — this points AWAY from a
  single-layer weight edit and TOWARD better data. (v2 had blocked at 18:54 UTC on
  per-token decode concatenation; the fix was tokenizer offset_mapping.)
- **Next: Experiment 5** (staged order /tmp/next-order-exp5.md, 00:32 +0545): alpha=0.5
  edited adapter WITH pen 1.2 — the last cheap test before better data. If it loses,
  next work is better data (curate high-quality Nepali examples, retrain LoRA).
  Do NOT run a full 52k training run.

  and duration gates, 959,936 frames were sent and matched, and pending frames,
  unmatched frames, RTP queue drops, and RTP write errors were all zero.

  Per-viewer p95 latency had a 1.034 s median (min 580 ms, max 2.079 s); p99
  median was 1.819 s. This remains a failed TEST proof, not a customer outcome.

  last-third slow fraction (86.0% to 38.3%) were lower, but forwarding was
  unchanged; treat this as run-to-run evidence, not a causal fix.
  There were 32,082 event gaps over 400 ms; the maximum per-viewer gap was
  5,464 ms. In the 56.6 s read sample, 71 `ReadRTP` calls took over 5 s and
  5,086 took 1–5 s; at 60.1 s, 10 took over 5 s and 1,963 took 1–5 s. The
  maximum sampled read duration was 5,343 ms.

  p99=9/max=13 across 3,000 subscriptions, with 90 non-empty and none full;
  other samples were at most 3 deep, and sampled NACK queues stayed empty.
  These five-second point samples show no sustained/full queue backlog but
  cannot exclude short-lived spikes between samples. Together with the long
  `ReadRTP` waits, this supports a late receive-path stall without identifying
  where packets stop arriving.
- **Transport reconciliation:** host-wide UDP counters changed by
  +6,133,797 received = +6,133,744 delivered +53 no-socket drops +0 full-buffer
  drops; datagram output increased by 6,097,140. The two 30-second intervals

  `logRouterFeedbackDiagnosis` path only emits them on a feedback failure, but

  logical NACK into reports of at most 253 pairs and sends each report in a

  errors. Individual writes avoid that; a focused test verifies all 512
  requested sequences survive, each report marshals below 1,500 bytes, and
  the combined form would exceed that buffer.
- **Owner action / action removed:** no owner action is needed to exercise
  this local feedback path. The router no longer passes oversized NACK report
  lists to Pion or combines the split reports into an oversized datagram.

  neither `too many reports` nor mux short-buffer errors, but stopped before

## 2026-11-16 — D85 cross-border export settlement (manual evidence; remains UNKNOWN)

### Primary rule set and version chronology

- Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB), Foreign Exchange Management Department, Unified Circular 11/2082-83, issued 2082/12/24 (7 April 2026), consolidates the prior circular and notices through that date. The PDF cover says Unified Circular 2082 although some inherited title/footer text still says 2081; preserve this version ambiguity rather than silently normalizing it. Export provisions are in the goods-export and service-export sections (PDF pages 65–70): https://www.nrb.org.np/contents/uploads/2026/04/for-upload-UC.pdf
- Later FXM amendments inspected: 12/2082-83 (9 June 2026), 1/2083-84 (23 July 2026), and 2/2083-84 (5 October 2026). The 23 July change concerns Indian banknotes; the 5 October amendment raises the cap for using already-received export proceeds to pay for imports from USD 12,000 to USD 30,000 for third-country imports and INR 30 lakh to INR 60 lakh for India. That is an import-payment facility funded by export proceeds, not a new export-receipt rail.
- The undated Trade and Export Promotion Centre export-procedure page describes advance payment and documentary credit as the two routes but exposes no effective date and is narrower than the later NRB circular, which also specifies CAD and service-export routes. Treat it as potentially incomplete guidance, not as the controlling current rule: https://tepc.gov.np/pages/exports-transit-procedure

### What the NRB circular actually permits

- Goods: an Advance Payment Certificate (APC) may be issued against foreign currency received through a bank with purpose/contract/order evidence. The evidence must identify the transaction and relevant origin/port/delivery details. Foreign-card online payments are also referenced through the separate card provisions. The bank that received the foreign currency issues the APC; if the exporter banks elsewhere, the receiving bank transfers the same currency and discloses fees. APC validity is up to two years, with specified renewal conditions.
- Letter of credit: banks can certify the export LC for customs when the exporter asks for negotiation or collection; banks monitor whether bills are presented and payment arrives. For documentary collection, the expected period cannot exceed six months from export; overdue cases are reported.
- Payment shortfalls: a bank may accept a shortfall up to 2% of document value or USD 1,000 (whichever is higher; INR 100,000 for INR) with the exporter's consent and supporting review. Larger shortfalls require NRB approval.
- Cash Against Documents (CAD): the specified CAD route applies to destinations other than India, up to USD 500,000 per shipment. It requires current firm/tax registration, invoice/contract/purchase order, insurance covering export value, and a 1% cash/deposit/security instrument. Payment must be received within six months; a bank guarantee requires prior NRB approval. Do not generalize this CAD route to India.
- Services: a Nepal-based firm/company/institution or natural person can receive service-export proceeds through licensed banks with PAN, invoice/purchase order where applicable, and an AML/CFT compliance self-declaration. The circular names SWIFT, draft/TT and other electronic payment instruments.

### Bank-level cost evidence

NMB Bank's Standard Tariff of Charges is explicitly effective 3 June 2026: https://backend.nmb.com.np/storage/download/2026/06/6871-STC%20-June%202026-Final%20Copy.pdf . Its export section lists, among other charges, LC advising NPR 1,000 plus NPR 2,000 authentication (refunded if export documents under the LC are presented at NMB), LC confirmation 0.50% per quarter or minimum NPR 5,000, clean sight export-bill negotiation 0.63% or minimum NPR 2,500, discrepant sight bills 0.75% or minimum NPR 2,500, CAD sight 0.25% or minimum NPR 2,500 plus courier/SWIFT, export-document handling NPR 2,500, export-payment follow-up NPR 1,000 plus SWIFT, CAD letter NPR 2,000, and APC NPR 1,000 per certificate. This is one bank's published tariff, not a market average or proof of what any exporter paid. Fixed minimums can dominate a small invoice; actual total charges depend on the chosen route, bank, correspondent charges and contract.

### Conclusion and Hami connection

The evidence does not support “cross-border payment is simply unavailable.” Several regulated routes exist, but eligibility, destination, payment method, documentation, collateral, deadlines and bank-specific minimum fees create a real decision surface. Whether payment is the binding constraint before product or logistics remains UNKNOWN: no exporter transaction cases, rejection rates, settlement times, or realized costs were obtained, and no people were contacted.

Represent this in the existing six primitives: exporter/buyer/bank/currency/payment instrument as Entities; contract, account and settlement links as Relations; invoice, advance receipt, APC, shipment, document negotiation, payment, shortfall and overdue as Events; NRB clause/version, bank tariff effective date, customs evidence and bank confirmations as Evidence; an evidence-backed route/document/fee/deadline checklist as a candidate Capability; any follow-up as an Action requiring owner authorization. This is a source-time/provenance test case as well as a trade question. No new model, collector, table, payment service or legal-advice claim is proposed. The next real-world dependency is consented transaction evidence across payment, logistics and product constraints, only after explicit owner authorization. NRB, TEPC and bank pages were manually inspected only; no robots/terms clearance or automated ingestion approval was inferred.

## 2026-11-16 — LiveKit Cloud guard and CI log minimization

- Official LiveKit documentation currently states Cloud load tests allow at most 50 each of video publishers, audio publishers and subscribers, and that test traffic counts against plan allowances. The CLI `--num-per-second` option is documented up to 10 participants/second; this is a CLI option limit, not a separate Cloud policy: https://docs.livekit.io/reference/developer-tools/livekit-cli/perf/
- The existing Cloud Compose defaults (10,000 subscribers and 100 joins/second) exceeded those documented bounds. The duplicated local `room_matches` helpers now log only room name, participant count and publisher count, not the complete Room object/ephemeral turnPassword.

## 2026-11-16 — production runtime truth and source-time provenance trace

### Production database and execution reality

- Exact deployment `dpl_7znHsW9PpExFWg9mYXVWHEKC6uRx` is READY, but Vercel project env list is empty (hidden production count 0). Runtime logs show HTTP 200 for `/api/health`, `/api/public/unknowns`, and `/api/payments/offers`; they also show `/tmp/forge.db`, `unknowns sync: inserted 124 new claims`, and `Legacy intelligence startup disabled.`
- `database.py` explicitly selects `sqlite:////tmp/forge.db` on Vercel when `DATABASE_URL` is absent and comments that rows live only for that instance. `main.py:on_startup` calls `init_db`; `init_db` invokes `sync_unknowns_from_map`; that service fetches the committed UNKNOWN_MAP and imports rows. Repeated 124-row insert logs are per-fresh-instance projection seeding, not new research evidence.
- `main.py:_health_details` classifies Vercel+SQLite as ephemeral and blocks readiness for missing durable DB and missing CRON_SECRET. `health()` returns HTTP 200 even when status is degraded; body not captured, so only code-derived status is recorded. `FORGEOS_LEGACY_INTELLIGENCE_ENABLED` is false. No unattended intelligence cycle is evidenced.
- The health failure path attempts to persist safe mode in the same per-instance SQLite database. It cannot be treated as a durable cross-instance HALT. The next dependency is owner-controlled durable DB/auth/scheduler configuration; no environment changes were made.

### Source-time trace through the existing seam

1. `backend/app/services/collectors/base.py`: `provenance = raw_item.get("provenance") or metadata`. A non-empty raw provenance object replaces normalized metadata rather than merging it.
2. `collector_runner.py`: preserves that provenance, adds task context and authorized source-registry identity, but does not merge every normalized metadata field into provenance.
3. `observer_engine.py`: stores only `metadata["provenance"]` on Signal; publication/retrieval timestamps go to separate columns. `_ensure_evidence` copies those fields to Evidence but does not populate the existing `Evidence.observed_at`.
4. Same-content dedup: if the content fingerprint is unchanged, ObserverEngine returns the prior Signal; `_ensure_evidence` returns existing Evidence. A newer source cutoff or retrieval timestamp may not refresh the existing record.
5. `research_evidence_assessment.py`: freshness is publication date compared with retrieval time. `research_synthesis_engine._evidence_citation`: exposes source/title/URL/registry ID/retrieved_at, not publication date or source-effective cutoff.
6. `models.py`: Signal/Evidence have published_at/retrieved_at/provenance; Evidence has observed_at but the collector writer leaves it unset. `RevenueSource.data_as_of` is specific to payout terms, not a generic evidence cutoff.

### Additive implementation plan (NOT IMPLEMENTED)

- Keep the existing Signal/Evidence models and provenance JSON.
- Merge normalized metadata with raw provenance deterministically, preserving source-provided values and existing registry/task provenance; never discard a non-empty raw provenance object or silently trust arbitrary top-level metadata.
- Add a namespaced source-time object only when the source actually declares it: raw label/value, calendar, timezone, precision, reporting period/scope, and parsed UTC only when conversion is justified. Missing/ambiguous values remain UNKNOWN.
- On unchanged content with changed metadata, retain a new retrieval observation or append-only provenance history instead of silently returning stale time metadata.
- Expose `published_at`, `retrieved_at`, and source-effective cutoff as distinct citation fields. Keep freshness assessment's basis explicit; do not substitute page publication date for data cutoff.
- Regression coverage: raw provenance plus metadata cutoff; missing/ambiguous calendar; unchanged body/new cutoff; same content/new retrieval; citation fields; unregistered source rejected; metadata not proof of claim support.
- No new model/table/primitive/collector is justified. The existing source-edit safety block remains; no source code changed.

### Rights and source registry

- Five registered source clearances are expired as of 16 Nov: GovInfo 2026-09-25; Crossref, World Bank, GDELT and OpenAlex 2026-10-27. The registry contains no NDRRMA entry. Keep all collectors fail-closed; re-review each source's robots, terms, purpose, fields, retention and provider scope independently.

## 2026-11-16 — LiveKit metric correction, Cloud harness safety, and D93 source-time correction

### LiveKit load-test semantics (verified against pinned upstream source)

- Hami pins `livekit/livekit-cli:v2.19.4`; that tag depends on `livekit/server-sdk-go/v2 v2.19.0`.
- [CLI loadtester.go](https://github.com/livekit/livekit-cli/blob/v2.19.4/pkg/loadtester/loadtester.go#L398-L424) increments its `dropped` counter from `samplebuilder.WithPacketDroppedHandler`. The accepted `packets` counter increments for each packet returned by `PopPackets`.
- [SampleBuilder.drop](https://github.com/livekit/server-sdk-go/blob/v2.19.0/pkg/samplebuilder/samplebuilder.go#L230-L247) calls the handler once per dropped frame, then releases the packets for that frame. The method is reached when the buffer is full or when an incomplete frame exceeds the `maxLate` sequence window.
- [CLI formatting](https://github.com/livekit/livekit-cli/blob/v2.19.4/pkg/loadtester/util.go#L34-L40) divides dropped callbacks by accepted packets plus callbacks. The printed `Pkt. Loss` percentage therefore mixes frame-drop events and RTP packet counts. It is not a valid network packet-loss percentage.
- Correction: the saved 250-subscriber result is **212 samplebuilder frame-drop callback events**, not 212 RTP packets; 0.005% is a mixed-unit CLI ratio. The 38 nonzero subscriber rows (34×6 callbacks, 4×2) and zero subscriber errors remain TEST observations; exact trigger per callback is unknown.
- Exact-head CI 43761793520 ran 9 publishers + 100 simulated subscribers, verified 109 participants and 600 video subscriptions, and all 100 subscriber rows reported 0 samplebuilder callbacks and no errors. This is a TEST harness result, not production capacity.
- Actual transport loss should use per-track inbound RTP `packets_lost` snapshots and interval deltas; [LiveKit stats docs](https://docs.livekit.io/robotics/media/performance/stats/) state the value is cumulative since subscription start. Hami has no capture-to-render measurement path; the 100 ms target remains NOT MEASURABLE.

### Cloud scale harness safety

- `docker-compose.livekit-scale.yml` targets LiveKit Cloud (`--project hami`) and defaults to 10,000 subscribers, 100 joins/second and five minutes. `scripts/livekit-scale-test.sh` defaults to 20 publisher containers. Its `test` subcommand fails closed after a Cloud rejection, but direct Compose invocation bypasses the script guard.
- Do not start Cloud publishers or the load-test service without explicit owner authorization and LiveKit written approval/approved procedure. No Cloud request or spend occurred.
- CI's `room_matches` helper prints the full Room JSON; observed logs include an ephemeral `turnPassword` field from the local test room. This is not evidence of production credential exposure, but is unnecessary secret-like logging. Next supported source change: print only allowlisted room name, participant count and publisher count; add/retain a regression that rejects secret-like fields in logs.

## 2026-11-15 — NSO WASH report body inspected; local baseline and service-chain crosswalk

### Source and source-time record
- Official NSO listing: https://www.nsonepal.gov.np/content/13536/water-supply-and-sanitation-sutuaion-in-nepal/ (page date 18 Kartik 2083).
- Full report PDF: https://giwmscdnone.gov.np/media/files/Water%20Supply%20and%20Sanitation%20Situation%20in%20Nepal_f9hdjvg.pdf .
- Keep distinct: NSO page/listing date (18 Kartik 2083); local-estimation period (2024/25); underlying local Census source/facility distributions (NPHC 2021); MICS transition-probability/benchmark period (2024/25); retrieval (2026-11-15). The report does not provide one universal current effective instant for every metric.
- Local JMP estimates combine Census 2021 distributions with transition probabilities from MICS 2024/25. Surface/unimproved drinking-water categories and the Census "No toilet" proxy for open defecation are directly Census-derived; remaining local JMP service categories are modelled. Do not call municipal values direct MICS observations.

### Verified findings
- National MICS 2024/25 scorecard: on-premises drinking water 90.0%; safely managed drinking water 47.5%; improved sanitation 92.8%; safely managed sanitation 39.9%; handwashing with water and soap 86.4%; open defecation 5.5%.
- Household water samples were E. coli-positive in 61.2%, compared with 46.1% of source samples. These are sample positivity rates, not population coverage; the difference does not by itself identify where contamination occurred.
- Safely managed drinking-water coverage is estimated below 50% in 518/753 local levels (68.8%); 348 are below 25%, 170 between 25–49%, 234 between 50–74%, and one at least 75%.
- Four planning categories cover 753 local levels: 57 P1 critical integrated WASH gap; 277 P2A drinking-water priority; 147 P2B sanitation priority; 272 P3 progress/sustain/learn. The 424 at-risk/inadequate local levels are not one homogeneous intervention group.
- Chumanubri RM, Gorkha: DWEI 0.529, SEI 0.670, WASH EI 0.595. Under the report's P1 band (0.376 ≤ WASH EI < 0.600), it falls in the critical integrated-gap planning category; the water index is lower than sanitation. These are index scores, not percentages of households served. This is a geographic cross-reference to D93's Gorkha context only: it does not establish flood damage or current disruption.
- The report says NPC's administrative safely managed-water estimate of 25.8% in 2022 and the MICS-based 47.5% for 2024/25 use different measurement approaches; this is not a confirmed 21.7-point service improvement.

### Method and uncertainty limits
- Direct model validation is only at national, provincial and 15 MICS analytical-domain levels; the report says direct district/municipality validation was not possible because MICS is not representative at that granularity.
- Qualitative field validation covered 33 local levels across 22 districts in six provinces. This is contextual triangulation, not direct representative validation of all 753 municipalities.
- Reported MAE: drinking water 1.57 percentage points nationally, 1.99 province, 2.22 at 15 domains; sanitation 3.61, 5.96 and 6.05 respectively. Do not transfer these validation errors to each municipality as a measured local confidence interval.
- The report identifies sampling uncertainty, Census-to-JMP classification uncertainty, and transferability uncertainty from assuming domain-level transition relationships apply within municipalities.
- WASH EI is the geometric mean of DWEI and SEI; it does not include hygiene. The report describes it as a foundation for a future broader WASH performance index, not a completed all-dimension WPI. Index scores are not household coverage percentages or permanent rankings.

### Practical value and existing Hami seam
- The evidence shifts attention from infrastructure counts alone to safe management, reliability, functionality, water quality, sanitation containment/treatment, operation and maintenance, and local institutional capacity.
- Reuse the six primitives: ENTITY (local government, scheme, source, operator, lab, funder, service area); RELATION (serves, owns, operates, funds, maintains, tests); EVENT (outage, sample, contamination result, repair, commissioning, emptying/treatment); EVIDENCE (source, date/period, method, unit, denominator, geography, uncertainty and rights); CAPABILITY (local service-chain and asset-to-need reconciliation); ACTION (internal review only unless separately authorized).
- This extends the existing source-time/evidence-graph seam; it is not a new model, table, primitive, collector, D-number or operational service. It can connect WASH baseline → asset/operator → dated condition/quality/repair record → funding/maintenance responsibility → measured service outcome.

It does not remove the need for current asset/operator records, local field verification, water-quality tests, service-interruption logs, budget/execution records or source-rights review.

Then assess whether existing provenance can carry source-time/method/uncertainty fields.

## 2026-11-14 — Governed Hami operator + LiveKit proving ground (design baseline; local harness scaffolded, runtime NOT VERIFIED)

### Mission translated into an engineering contract
- One Hami, extending the existing system. No second agent, parallel ledger, new semantic primitive, or replacement runtime.
- Durable intent → reasoning → registered capability → execution-time authority → tool invocation → independent postcondition verification → evidence/outcome → reusable method.
- “Inner power” means Hami owns its mission, reasoning process, durable memory, plans, controls and recovery. External sources and machines remain necessary to observe and affect the physical world; they do not own Hami's identity.
- Zero compromise means fail-closed truth, authorization, privacy, security, audit and verification. It does not mean claiming infinite resources, zero latency or flawless software.

### Verified run-start state
- Main at inspection: `6267be567194750044f78a6808d76501c1fe9b88`. Latest commit at that point: `6267be567194750044f78a6808d76501c1fe9b88` (`fix(hami): retain Ollama goal planning call metrics`).
- Workflow run `43615184838` for that exact SHA was still in progress at inspection. Build, lint, typecheck, frontend tests, route smoke, repository guards, evidence-triage tests and secret scan had completed successfully; backend tests remained in progress. Do not call the exact-head suite green until the backend job and overall run complete.
- Hami has an owner-only goal-planning route, strict proposal-only GoalPlan contract, replaceable cognition provider, existing WorkerTask persistence and a narrow proposal-only handler. Goal planning is not general task execution.
- Existing `action_engine.py` provides a canonical Action lifecycle and adapter registry. `decision_rights.py` defaults unknown action types to OWNER_ONLY. Execution revalidates relevant rights/standing authorization before adapter dispatch. This is the execution seam to extend.
- `worker_manager.py` has durable task claiming/retry logic, but most worker execution remains behind the legacy-intelligence flag. Its builder and QA handlers explicitly report that they did not build or inspect an artifact.
- `tool_registry.py` currently describes/selects registered intelligence/source tools; it is not a general-purpose browser, shell or infrastructure executor. Root Playwright scripts are currently browser smoke/QA with a local-target guard, not a full autonomous browser.
- No LiveKit server, streamer containers, SFU cluster, load generator, 4,000-viewer run or 100ms measurement was provisioned in this inspection.
- The latest READY Vercel production deployment is SHA `6076690f00c238f1b22a3afcdf489e983c468e7d`, not the inspected main SHA. No deployment record existed for the inspected SHA. `https://haminp.vercel.app/api/health` returned HTTP 402 `DEPLOYMENT_DISABLED`; current production health is NOT VERIFIED. No billing, usage, resume, deployment or spend setting was changed.

### Existing seams; missing link
- Goal understanding/planning: `Goal`, `GoalPlan`, `goal_engine.py`, `cognitive_provider.py`, `WorkerTask`.
- Governed execution: `Action`, `action_engine.py`, `decision_rights.py`, `autonomy_engine.py`, existing Action/Event/audit records.
- Persistent work: `worker_manager.py`, existing scheduler and `WorkerTask` retry/idempotency fields.
- Capability discovery: existing `ToolRegistry` and `ForgeCapability`.
- Browser: existing Playwright dependency and browser smoke scripts; needs a bounded read-only browser adapter with host/path allowlists and no ambient credentials.
- Missing integration: validated GoalPlan steps are not yet mapped to registered Actions/adapters and dispatched through the existing authorization + verification path. Do not let model-generated strings become shell commands, URLs, permissions or provider credentials.

### Build order (reuse existing files and primitives)
1. **Exact-head quality gate.** Finish the current backend test run; diagnose failures from logs; verify CI against the exact SHA. Keep Vercel `DEPLOYMENT_DISABLED` separate from code-test results.
2. **Governed executor in the existing Action seam.** Define a closed, typed allowlist of internal operations; map plan steps to known action types; validate parameters; check rights and scope immediately before execution; persist start/result/error; verify a deterministic postcondition independently. Unknown tools, malformed inputs, expired grants, HALT, timeouts or ambiguity must fail closed. No generic unrestricted shell.
3. **Persistent worker reliability.** Extend existing `WorkerTask`/scheduler path for lease/heartbeat, stale-running recovery, idempotent execution, bounded retry/backoff, cancellation, resource limits and failure-only operator escalation. Do not silently enable all legacy workers.
4. **First operating tools.** Begin with bounded, read-only repository inspection; fixed test/build commands in an isolated workspace; then read-only browser research against explicitly cleared/allowlisted hosts. Add write-capable adapters only with a specific permission envelope and rollback/test plan.
5. **Resource independence.** Separate control plane from workers. Use one heavy local model at a time; initially cap browser concurrency at one; pause noncritical work under memory pressure. Docker isolates processes but does not create additional host RAM/CPU. Add remote workers only after a provider-independent deployment and spend decision.
6. **LiveKit proving ground.** Hami should calculate the media topology and bandwidth before provisioning; generate reproducible configuration; validate it; deploy only in an authorized environment; load-test; independently inspect metrics and recover from worker failure. Preserve the LiveKit configuration, test recipe and verified capacity in Hami's existing evidence/capability records so a repeat task becomes a known playbook rather than a fresh invention.

### LiveKit capacity math (planning assumptions, not a benchmark)
- LiveKit's self-hosted distributed mode scales many rooms across nodes, but each individual room must fit on one node. Official self-hosted guidance says roughly up to 3,000 participants in a room; 9 publishers + 4,000 viewers is 4,009 participants and is outside that guidance. A second SFU node does not transparently split one self-hosted room. See official benchmark and distributed-mode docs.
- At an illustrative 720p stream rate of 1.5 Mbps:
  - One selected stream per viewer: `4,000 × 1.5 Mbps ≈ 6 Gbps` outbound media.
  - Nine simultaneous streams per viewer: `4,000 × 9 × 1.5 Mbps ≈ 54 Gbps` outbound media.
  - Nine publishers ingesting one 1.5 Mbps rendition each: `9 × 1.5 Mbps ≈ 13.5 Mbps` inbound, before simulcast layers/audio/protocol overhead.
- These are arithmetic scenarios, not capacity claims. LiveKit states actual SFU capacity depends on published tracks, subscriber count and bytes forwarded per subscriber; its reference video benchmark used a 16-core compute-optimized GCP machine, not the local development laptop.
- Candidate paths to test, not preselected outcomes:
  1. Hami logical-room control plane with multiple bounded LiveKit media rooms (audience sharding) and an explicitly designed publisher-track relay; this changes media topology and requires unified chat/presence semantics.
  2. Managed global-mesh service as a measured comparison only; cost, usage limits, terms and provider dependence must be explicit.
  3. Do not claim that simply running multiple self-hosted SFU containers makes a single room larger.
- Define the latency SLO before benchmarking: capture-to-render glass-to-glass p50/p95/p99, geography, resolution/codec, audio/video track count, loss, jitter, reconnect time and viewer layout. “100ms” without a measurement definition and geographic scope is not a testable guarantee.
- Use LiveKit's `lk perf load-test`/equivalent generators from separate machines for large tests; generators themselves need CPU, bandwidth and file handles. Cloud load-test allowances are restricted. No 4,000-viewer test or paid Cloud test until the account/plan and cost are owner-approved.

### “Boom next time” equation
- Autonomous success requires every link: `durable intent × permitted tools × execution-time authority × independent verification × recovery`. If any factor is zero, the end-to-end autonomous result is zero.
- Repeat speed: `T_next = plan_lookup + resource_start + execution + verification`. Reduce plan lookup and resource start with saved, tested playbooks, prebuilt images, cached configuration, warm workers and measured resource scheduling. Never remove verification to make a demo look instant.

### Acceptance criteria
- A goal can be converted into typed Actions without executing during planning.
- Every Action is idempotent, permission-checked at dispatch, scoped to an allowlisted target, and produces durable evidence of result/error.
- Independent verifier reopens/checks the actual artifact or service; provider acceptance or a model's claim is not proof.
- Crash/restart, duplicate dispatch, timeout, stale lease, resource pressure, HALT and unauthorized target tests all fail safely or recover deterministically.
- The LiveKit benchmark records actual hardware, room topology, publishers, subscribers, active tracks/view layout, bitrate, aggregate ingress/egress, CPU/RAM, packet loss, jitter and capture-to-render latency distribution. Capacity is reported only at a tested load with headroom.
- No production deployment, billing/usage change, external communication, paid infrastructure or permission widening is implied by this design record.

Runtime status is **NOT RUN / NOT VERIFIED** until executed on an authorized Docker host.
- **No scale claim:** the scaffold is only a local TEST harness. It does not demonstrate 4,000 viewers, nine production camera feeds, room sharding/relay, or 100 ms glass-to-glass latency. ## 2026-11-14 — Hami universal goal interpretation v1 (implemented; exact-head CI pending)

### Capability added
- Added an owner-only `POST /forge/goals/{goal_id}/plan` path that turns an existing active Goal into a durable, idempotent `WorkerTask`; the task captures the exact goal revision so a changed goal cannot silently reuse a stale plan.
- Extended the existing replaceable cognition provider with a distinct general-goal planning contract. The provider receives the human objective, optional target metric and declared capability metadata. It must return bounded success criteria, assumptions, unknowns, evidence needed, capability gaps, ordered steps, permissions, blockers and independent verification requirements.
- The strict schema rejects execution authority, invalid step ordering and an unavailable result containing steps. Every plan and every step is explicitly non-executable. The deterministic MOCK adapter returns `UNAVAILABLE`, not a fabricated plan. Ollama uses the existing shared `ai_engine` provider and its established data-boundary checks; no parallel model stack was added.
- Reused Goal, WorkerTask/idempotency, ToolRegistry metadata, WorldEvent/type registry, existing owner API authentication, and the operating-v4 dormancy guard. No new table, top-level primitive, ledger, provider stack, scheduler or route family was introduced.
- Added TEST coverage for persistent idempotency, replacement-provider planning, no Action creation, mock honesty, authority/order rejection, non-proposal worker gating, and the actual Ollama JSON-provider adapter path. These tests are not REAL deployment or load-test evidence.

### Evidence boundary and remaining gaps
- Main HEAD at this entry: `6fe1bbbcf432e07a132674873d3cd1bc4dd62bd5`. Frontend tests, evidence-triage tests, lint, build, typecheck, repository guards, route smoke and Gitleaks passed on exact head. Backend pytest was still running when this entry was prepared; final status must be taken from GitHub Actions, not inferred.

### Source-backed finding and time boundaries

It says public-transport operators often rely on independent workshops after vehicle warranties expire, raising service-quality, safety and long-term-reliability concerns. The 7 April 2026 Harit Yatra Sambaad dialogue identified insufficient EV laboratories, training vehicles and qualified instructors. This is a project assessment and stakeholder dialogue, not a national census or firsthand service-failure dataset.
- The same 16 June article records CTEVT Director Binod Badal's statement that CTEVT has introduced a 390-hour short course and a 1,696-hour professional EV-technician course, while implementation is constrained by infrastructure, practical EV access and instructor capacity. It says SET4NPL intends to train 100 mechanics in 2026; this is a target, not a completion count.
- CTEVT's official [Professional EV Technician curriculum](https://ctevt.org.np/uploads/docs/2026-04-16_Professional_EV_Technician_1696%20Hrs._2024.pdf) identifies itself as a 2024, competency-based 1,696-hour programme. It covers two-, three- and four-wheelers, diagnostics, high-voltage power control, charging systems, high-voltage battery packs, thermal systems, motors, brakes and other vehicle systems. It specifies a maximum of 20 trainees per group, 12 weeks of on-the-job training, and a 1:10 practical instructor-to-trainee ratio. The document proves a curriculum exists; it does not prove that a current cohort is running, that graduates exist, or that graduates are employed.
- CTEVT's [training-portal record for Electric Vehicle Technician](https://ctevt.org.np/trainingportal/public/program/569/EVtech) lists a separate 390-hour sponsored/free course at Shankharapur Polytechnic Institute, Shankhu-6, Kathmandu: deadline 16 March 2026, start 22 March, end 14 June, quota 20. This 390-hour course is not equivalent to the 1,696-hour CTEVT professional curriculum or the 60-hour SET4NPL upskilling courses.
- GGGI Nepal's official [company update feed](https://np.linkedin.com/company/gggi-nepal), retrieved 14 November, reports the second 60-hour EV Skills Upgradation cohort at BKG Engineering Workshop, Pokhara, from 23 September to 4 October 2026, with 27 participants. ### Real-world consequence and affected entities

The affected network includes public-transport operators and passengers, independent mechanics/workshops, vehicle suppliers and authorised service networks, training providers and CTEVT, VFTC and government inspection officials, and charging operators. The documented concern is the transition from warranty-backed supplier service to independent repair capacity. If qualified, equipped independent workshops are unavailable when warranties expire, repair delay, poor-quality work, safety risk and vehicle downtime may follow. The assessment identifies those as concerns; this pass found no measured incident rate, repair failure, downtime, injury, warranty-expiry cohort or economic loss. No operational coordination failure is claimed.

### Independent corroboration, limits and unresolved wording

- The MAF/SET4NPL assessment, dialogue and GGGI project updates are one related project/source family, not independent national measurements. CTEVT's curriculum and training-portal record independently establish formal training resources. Paramount Motors' listing is a separate employer demand signal. The 400-bus figure remains project-reported.
- The 60-hour SET4NPL upskilling cohorts, 390-hour CTEVT short course and 1,696-hour CTEVT professional curriculum are distinct programmes. Their participant counts and credentials must not be combined as if they were equivalent qualifications.
- The 18 VFTC officials are inspectors/regulators, not mechanic trainees.
- The CTEVT portal's zero-applicant display is not reliable enough to infer an unused training resource because its timestamp/definition are absent and the page reports a storage error.
- SET4NPL's maintenance-contract summary versus optional-contract wording is unresolved. Do not infer that every supported bus has a maintenance contract, charger, post-warranty service coverage or a particular battery-replacement entitlement.
- Unknown: actual completion/certification and OJT placement for all cohorts; progress against the 100-mechanic target after the documented 52; delivery of the 1,696-hour curriculum; number, geography, skills, tools and authorisations of independent EV workshops; service coverage after warranty; vehicle-specific contract terms and uptake; parts/battery repair capacity; service incidents, downtime, costs and safety outcomes; and employer demand beyond the one vacancy. No mechanic, operator, workshop or passenger was interviewed.

### Reusable Hami capability and existing code seam

A reusable capability candidate is to reconcile the service/workforce chain: training provider and cohort → competencies and practical equipment → OJT/completion/certification → workshop capability and location → employer requirements → vehicle/fleet and warranty/maintenance contract → service event and observed outcome. This could expose where existing training, skills, service resources and fleet needs do or do not connect, and help route people toward training or work without inventing a marketplace or assuming a buyer. It could also help public-transport operators and institutions see whether post-warranty support is actually available. No willingness-to-pay or commercial demand is established.

Reuse only the six canonical primitives and existing substrate: ENTITY for institutions, workshops, operators, suppliers and vehicles; RELATION for training, employment, maintenance and service links; EVENT for cohort, OJT, warranty, maintenance and service milestones; EVIDENCE for source/version/scope/time/claim support; CAPABILITY for verified skills and equipment; ACTION only after authorization.

D86 asks how much FY2082/83's “+18% export growth” is re-processed palm oil (+246.7%) versus broad-based capacity. The source review shows that the question combines three different measures:

- Nepal Rastra Bank's official [nine-month FY2025/26 report](https://www.nrb.org.np/contents/uploads/2026/05/CMEFs_Eng_Nine-Months_2082.83.pdf), published 11 May 2026 and based on data ending mid-April, reports merchandise exports +18.5% to Rs222.94b. It says exports to India +22.6%, other countries +5.1%, China −46.8%; soybean oil, cardamom, palm oil, jute goods and noodles increased, while zinc sheet, particle board, tea, wool carpet and handicrafts decreased. In its BEC classification, exports were 69.4% final-consumption goods, 29.8% intermediate goods and 0.8% capital goods. This is a nine-month period, not the FY2082/83 annual total.
- The official [Department of Customs FY2082/83 foreign-trade page](https://customs.gov.np/content/450/foreign-trade-statistics-came-208-83/) is dated 7 Sawan 2083 and links the Asar-to-year-end workbook. The primary XLSX at https://giwmscdnone.gov.np/media/files/FTS_Upto_Ashadh_82_83_gdfkmo9.xlsx was not extractable in this run; no direct HS-level values were re-read from the primary workbook.
- The 30 Sep 2026 [24Ghanta article](https://www.24ghantanepal.com/article/nepals-trade-shift-in-fy-208283-imports-rise-in-value-as-processed-oil-and-agricultural-products-drive-export-growth) reports the top-ten export basket rising from Rs18,169 crore to Rs21,433 crore (+18%), with processed palm oil +246.7% and cardamom +64.6%. Its 18% is the top-ten basket, not total annual exports. It names the Department of Customs as its source but does not publish the underlying HS crosswalk or item-level rupee values.
- The independent, privately operated [Customs Nepal refined-edible-oils page](https://www.customsnepal.com/sector/edible-oils-exports), updated 12 Nov 2026, attributes its trade figures to Department of Customs FY2082/83 data and discloses that its sector is a selected HS-code basket, not an official classification. It reports refined edible oils at Rs149b, +21%, or 47.2% of annual exports; soybean oil (HS 1507.90.00) Rs129b / 86.5% of the sector; palm olein (1511.90.20) Rs6.67b, up Rs5.11b (+328%); refined palm oil (1511.90.10) Rs1.69b, up Rs0.866b (+105%); sunflower oil Rs8.94b, down Rs3.38b (−27%). The broader three-line palm group is approximately Rs8.36b versus Rs2.42b, about +Rs5.94b; the article's +246.7% group definition is not exactly reconciled to the aggregator's HS grouping. It reports almost all refined-edible-oil exports going to India and Rs176b of imports under the same sector's selected codes.
- The same private compilation reports total FY2082/83 merchandise exports around Rs315b, +13.8%. Therefore the annual total, NRB's nine-month +18.5%, and the article's top-ten +18% must remain separate. The top-ten Rs214.33b basket is about 68% of the compiled Rs315b total; this is a cross-source estimate, not a primary official cross-tab.
- NRB's official [two-month FY2026/27 report](https://www.nrb.org.np/red/current-macroeconomic-and-financial-situation-english-based-on-two-months-data-of-2026-27/current-macroeconomic-and-financial-situation-english-based-on-two-months-data-of-2026-27/), published 15 Oct 2026 with data through mid-September, reports exports +61.9% to Rs76.59b. Soybean oil, polyester yarn/thread, palm oil, zinc sheet and particle board increased; several other product groups declined. BEC export composition was 71.1% final-consumption, 28.8% intermediate and 0.1% capital goods. This period ends before India's 24 Sep edible-oil tariff change.
- [OnlineKhabar's 28 Oct first-quarter account](https://english.onlinekhabar.com/nepals-exports-cross-114-billion.html), citing Department of Customs, reports FY2083/84 mid-July–mid-October exports of Rs114.28b (+57.03%), vegetable-oil exports Rs59.32b and crude vegetable-oil raw-material imports Rs66.66b. It also reports Rs95.59b of exports to India. This is secondary reporting, not an extracted primary workbook. The period straddles the 24 Sep Indian duty change, so the aggregate cannot identify its effect.
- Reuters' [23 Sep 2026 report](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/india-cuts-import-duty-palm-oil-soyoil-sunflower-oil-2026-09-23/) says India reduced basic duties effective 24 Sep: crude palm/soybean 10%→5%, refined palm/soybean 32.5%→27.5%, crude sunflower 10%→0%, refined sunflower 32.5%→22.5%. The primary Indian notification body was not retrieved in this pass. Treat this as an external risk/possible incentive change, not a measured cause of Nepal's post-change exports.

### What the evidence does and does not establish

- “+18%” is not a single FY2082/83 total-export growth figure. It refers to the top-ten basket; NRB's 18.5% is a separate nine-month figure; the annual total is reported around +13.8%.
- Palm's +246.7% is a percentage rate on a much smaller base. The available HS-level values show soybean oil's roughly Rs21.95b absolute increase is about 3.7 times the combined Rs5.94b increase across the two main refined-palm lines. The phrase “biggest contributor” is therefore ambiguous: palm has the highest percentage growth, while soybean oil is the larger absolute rupee driver in this breakdown.
- Refined edible oils' reported 47.2% share and near-total India destination indicate product and destination concentration. Crude-oil imports alongside refined-oil exports are consistent with an import-feedstock processing/re-export channel. They do not establish batch-level input/output matching, domestic value added, margins, employment, number of refiners/exporters, beneficial ownership, origin-rule compliance, or resilience.
- BEC categories are statistical product-use categories, not a direct measure of domestic productive capacity. A small capital-goods export share does not prove absence of manufacturing capability. Some non-oil product groups grew; others declined. Broad-based capacity remains unproven rather than disproven.
- No official HS workbook extraction, firm-level concentration, local input share, processing yield, tariff pass-through, post-24-Sep monthly series, or exporter employment/outcome data was established. D86 remains UNKNOWN.

### Existing Hami seam, reusable capability and priority

- **ENTITY:** Department of Customs, NRB, commodity/HS lines, importers/refiners/exporters, destination markets, Indian tariff authority and affected industries.
- **RELATION:** imports-feedstock-for-processing; refines/exports; exports-to-destination; tariff-applies-to-HS-line. Keep the actual firms, ownership, origin and contract relationships UNKNOWN unless directly evidenced.
- **EVENT:** fiscal-period trade observations, Customs report publication, NRB report publication, tariff effective date and monthly shipment observations.
- **EVIDENCE:** retain exact publisher, URL, publication date, source-declared data period/cutoff, retrieval date, HS definition, unit, denominator, geography, revision/version and rights state separately.
- **CAPABILITY:** fiscal-period-aware trade-series reconciliation and concentration decomposition, reusable for disaster reports, energy project timelines, WASH surveys and other source series.
- **ACTION:** internal analysis only. No contact, supplier outreach, public claim, alert or commercial action is authorized by this evidence.
- Existing code path: `SourceCollector.normalize → collector_runner.execute_task → ObserverEngine.observe/_ensure_evidence → Signal → Evidence → research_evidence_assessment.assess_source_record → research_synthesis_engine._evidence_citation`. Signal/Evidence already store `published_at`, `retrieved_at` and `provenance`. Freshness currently compares publication date with retrieval time. An explicit `raw_item.provenance` can displace normalized metadata; citation output does not expose a source-declared effective period/cutoff or full metric scope. Typed Claim/EvidenceRelationship links exist, but metadata linkage is not proof that source body substantiates a claim.
- **Prepared change, NOT IMPLEMENTED:** preserve a structured `source_time` object inside existing provenance: raw time label; role (publication, data cutoff, period, event time); calendar; period start/end or exact as-of instant; timezone and precision; source scope; unit/denominator/metric/HS definition; source version/local ID. Merge explicit provenance with normalized metadata without dropping either. Carry the object through Signal, Evidence, assessment and citation. Report publication age separately from data-period age; missing or ambiguous time stays UNKNOWN. Never infer claim support from a date, URL or metadata link.
- **Regression coverage to add when the supported source-edit path exists:** explicit provenance does not erase normalized source metadata; source-time round-trips through Signal/Evidence; publication date differs from period end; missing cutoff stays UNKNOWN; period boundaries and source revisions remain distinct; conflicting periods remain visible; citations expose source time without marking claim support. Existing tests cover missing publication dates and typed support/contradiction, not these cases.
- **Exact blocker:** the previously proposed source write in `research_planner.py` remains blocked by source-edit safety. No alternative write path was used. No new model, table, collector, primitive, task, D-number or parallel ledger.
- **Owner dependency removed:** no owner intervention was needed to correct the denominator/period interpretation and identify the concentration risk. The remaining dependency is a supported source-edit path plus direct primary-workbook extraction and rights review, not another vision or seller experiment.
- **Priority:** high reuse and low research cost; moderate interpretation risk because the annual HS workbook was not extracted and several values are secondary. Continue independent tracks while source editing remains blocked.

## [2026-11-02 — D95 agriculture market-coordination subcase: AMPIS measurement comparability; farm-to-retail chain remains unresolved]

- **Official market system and scope:** the Government of Nepal's [AMPIS homepage](https://ampis.gov.np/) displayed its daily wholesale list and cross-market comparison dated Kartik 15, 2083 when retrieved on 2 Nov 2026. The [market directory](https://ampis.gov.np/contact-us) lists 12 centres; the [commodity directory](https://www.ampis.gov.np/available-commodity) lists 170 commodity records. These are market-level wholesale records, not farmgate prices, retail prices, delivered prices, or farmer net returns. The accessible pages do not state a retrieval/observation time-of-day.
- **Primary method finding:** AMPIS's official [technical note](https://www.ampis.gov.np/technical-note) says the original 11 market centres collect five daily prices per commodity from traders/farmers, but the data-entry format has not captured all observations. The published representative value is therefore the midpoint of minimum and maximum: (min + max) / 2. Kalimati was added from 2083 Asar 1 and calculates an arithmetic mean from multiple observations. The note explicitly warns that midpoint and arithmetic-mean indicators are not fully directly comparable and says the system plans to transition all markets toward multi-observation means. The note's own publication/update date is not displayed; its stated method and planned transition are source claims, not proof the transition has since occurred.
- **Current comparison-table artifact:** the Kartik 15 table for “large Nepali tomato” shows repeated market labels (including Kamalamai, Butwal, Dharan and Attariya) and two different Pokhara rows. The page does not explain whether these are separate reporting groups, multiple submissions, or duplicate records. Preserve UNKNOWN; do not deduplicate, call it a confirmed data error, or treat the displayed “average” values as one estimator. The page lists Kalimati at Rs 60–70/kg (average Rs 65) alongside other centres, but AMPIS's own note says the Kalimati mean and the other centres' midpoints are not directly comparable.
- **Real-world consequence and affected entities:** farmers, traders, market committees, wholesalers, retailers, consumers and analysts may misread spatial price differences or trends if the common “average” label is taken to mean the same calculation everywhere. This is a documented comparability limitation, not evidence that a person made a wrong decision, that arbitrage exists, or that a coordination failure has occurred.
- **Separate supply-chain context, not a joined chain:** [The Kathmandu Post, 28 Sep 2026](https://kathmandupost.com/money/2026/09/28/nepal-s-broken-supply-chain-farmers-earn-less-consumers-pay-more) attributes to government studies an example of farmers in Makawanpur/Dhading receiving Rs 25–35/kg for vegetables sold for up to Rs 125/kg at Kathmandu retail, and reports up to seven market layers. That example's arithmetic is about 3.6–5 times; the article's “up to seven times” is a broader separate claim. The underlying study and same-lot records were not retrieved. Nepal Rastra Bank's [15 Oct 2026 two-month macroeconomic release](https://www.nrb.org.np/) reports 6.34% national CPI and 7.54% food-and-beverage inflation at mid-September; this is independent macro context, not corroboration of a vegetable-specific margin or the farmgate example. These sources differ in period, geography and measure.
- **Unresolved dimensions:** observation count and sampling frame per market; meaning of repeated rows; commodity grade/size/origin equivalence; observation window and timestamp; farmgate transaction price; transport, handling, fees, grading, spoilage, labour, storage, credit and commission costs; retail price for the same commodity/batch; and whether the stated method transition has happened. No firsthand farmer, trader or retailer evidence and no user-demand evidence were obtained.
- **Capability candidate:** method-aware price and value-chain reconciliation using only the six existing primitives. ENTITY: commodity/grade, market, route and participants. RELATION: commodity-to-market/route and participant-to-transaction. EVENT: dated price observation, transfer and sale. EVIDENCE: exact source, market identity, unit, grade/origin, source date/cutoff, estimator, sample count and min/max/mean. CAPABILITY: compare only when method, product and scope are compatible; otherwise expose the incompatibility. ACTION: later consented/authorized verification only. AMPIS already supplies a public market-price surface; Hami should not duplicate it or claim a new market platform is needed.
- **Existing Hami code seam:** at run-start SHA `3cb14cd0a50e1bc79c516c7f85f9d67861581d12`, the path was traced as `SourceCollector.normalize → collector_runner.execute_task → ObserverEngine.observe → _ensure_evidence → assess_source_record → _evidence_citation`. `normalize` returns `raw_item.provenance or metadata`; the runner enriches provenance but does not merge every nested metadata field; ObserverEngine persists top-level provenance and Evidence inherits it. Assessment currently compares publication with retrieval time; synthesis citation exposes registry identity/retrieval time but not publication/effective cutoff, report version or measurement method. This is a contract risk, not demonstrated production data loss. A future permitted extension should preserve an allowlisted source-declared estimator/sample/scope alongside existing source-time provenance; no new model, table, primitive or collector is justified.
- **Rights and action boundary:** `https://ampis.gov.np/robots.txt` was inaccessible through the browser route; that tool-level failure is not an allow or deny response. No terms or content-reuse grant was found on the reviewed pages; the footer says © 2026 / all rights reserved. AMPIS has no entry in `docs/PUBLIC_SOURCES.md` or `source_clearance_registry.py`. Status: NOT CLEARED for automated collection, persistent storage or provider transmission. Manual page review only; no collector, Signal/Evidence write, source-body persistence, provider transmission or external contact.

- **D94 event/scope:** the 29 Oct 2026 Sintaphu/Shintaphu Lake GLOF in Gasa, Bhutan is distinct from the 26 Aug Rasuwa–Bhotekoshi and 11 Oct Gorkha–Budhi Gandaki events. ICIMOD's 30 Oct release estimates 6–7 million m³ in the original glacial lake before the outburst; the released volume remains under assessment. NewsOnAir's NCHM-advisory report displays 30 Oct 14:25 and was updated 31 Oct. It describes a second, debris-formed artificial lake at Taktsemakhang, at the confluence of Sintaphu Chhu and Lungu Chhu (also called Gangchen Tag Chhu), and monitoring/advisory coverage for the Mochhu and Punatsangchhu valleys. This 30 Oct advisory is about the secondary lake; it is not the time of the initial 29 Oct warning.
- **Reported event/observation/alert chronology:** The Times of India (31 Oct 02:41 IST), attributing data to NCHM, says floodwater crossed Taktsemakhang at about 20:27 on 29 Oct; sirens along Mochhu and downstream Punatsangchhu were activated as stations recorded a sharp rise; Yebesa peaked at 6.7 m at 23:00 and had receded to 2.84 m around 00:30 on 30 Oct. SANDRP reports the crossing at about 20:15; this 12-minute difference is unresolved and both reports are secondary. Exact timezone for the event/station times is not stated. No raw station trace or exact siren/alarm time was retrieved. The NCHM advisory at 30 Oct 14:25 must not be mistaken for the initial warning timestamp.
- **CWC advisory timing:** New Indian Express says the CWC special advisory was issued on 29 Oct; SANDRP describes it as issued in the early hours of 30 Oct and reproduces a DD News Assamese post dated 29 Oct. Exact original CWC issue time and the direct advisory were not retrieved. Treat the date boundary as unresolved, not as a proven contradiction or operational delay.
- **Impact/corroboration:** Reuters (30 Oct 02:53 UTC), citing BBS/Kuensel, reports evacuation before the flood, no deaths/injuries reported at that time, damage at Gasa Tshachu, an impassable road to Laya and two Bailey bridges possibly swept away. The Times of India (31 Oct) reports one Bailey bridge in Punakha and damage to Gasa-Laya/Punakha-Gasa road sections; bridge count is unresolved. New Indian Express (30 Oct 13:04) reports more than 10,000 relocated in Alipurduar and no official deaths/injuries by Friday afternoon. The Times of India later reports 18 shelters, about 10,000 people from Alipurduar plus a couple thousand from Assam, and people returning after the Sankosh receded. These are media-reported, time-bounded figures; no consolidated official evacuation/return register was retrieved.
- **Downstream gauges (secondary reproduction only):** SANDRP's 30 Oct article/31 Oct postscript reproduces CWC readings: Sankosh LRP 44.54 m at 17:00 (0.62 m rise between 07:00 and 10:00); Golokganj 27.1 m at 17:00 (1.84 m below warning); Baladoba 25.43 m at 18:00 (5.27 m below HFL). It describes the latter two Assam stations as stable and says it is unclear whether the surge had reached or passed them. The Times of India reports a roughly 1.5 m Sankosh rise followed by recession. These observations have different stations, times and reference levels; they are not directly comparable and no contradiction is established. SANDRP's 31 Oct postscript attributes gradual secondary-lake recession and three controlled explosions to a post by The Bhutanese editor; no official confirmation was retrieved.
- **Historical operating design, not 2026 performance:** NCHM's official GLOF EWS SOP v3.0 (March 2021) documents 10 AWLS, 4 AWS, 18 sirens and telemetry to Wangdue; Taktsemakhang (below Laya) is listed as AWLS+AWS on the Mochhu, with Tashithang and Yebesa further downstream. It specifies a 24/7 control room, daily telemetry/siren-signal checks, quarterly/annual inspections and facility logbooks. The information-flow procedure requires each operations-log entry to record sender, transmission time, recipient and receipt time; the warning chain includes DDM/dzongkhags, vulnerable communities and PHPA-I, PHPA-II and Basochhu. The SOP places Taktsemakhang about 70 km upstream of Punakha Dzong.
- **Lead-time/threshold correction:** SOP section 2.2 distinguishes gross lead (detection to flood arrival at the point of interest) from net lead (time left for protective action after forecasting/warning preparation). The 3–4 hour Taktsemakhang-to-Punakha estimate is approximate gross lead, not net public action time, not a measured 2026 window and not a current forecast. The SOP says breach volume, artificial dams and debris affect lead time; this event formed a secondary debris blockage, so the historical estimate is not transferable. The SOP also says thresholds may change with physical conditions at monitoring sites. Do not compare the reported 2026 Yebesa 6.7 m peak to the 2021 7.0 m alarm threshold or infer whether an alarm should have triggered.
- **Finding, not failure:** NCHM-attributed reporting of siren activation and downstream alerts is positive operational evidence. The expert quoted by the Times of India says timely activation prevented loss of life; that is an attributed causal opinion, not a verified counterfactual. No sensor failure, coordination failure, exact recipient delivery, causal prevented-loss outcome, current lake clearance or current restoration status is established. NCHM/TOI's confluence naming (Sintaphu Chhu/Lungu Chhu/Gangchen Tag Chhu) and SANDRP's Shingchala Chhu blockage reference need geospatial verification; treat as unresolved naming/location, not a proven conflict.
- **Consequence and affected entities:** Laya access, the Punakha–Gasa highway, Gasa Tshachu, downstream settlements in Punakha/Wangdue and the Sankosh corridor, evacuation shelters, NCHM/DDM/CWC and hydropower operators are in the event chain.
